scenario.title: Restoring a school occupied by armed actors

agreed_facts: A primary school serving around 1,000 displaced and host-community children is partially occupied by approximately 40 to 50 fighters
Children face fear, restricted movement and protection risks including potential sexual violence
The presence of armed actors prevents humanitarian support to regular education programming
contested_facts: Whether the armed actors' presence is a protection problem or a protection guarantee
Whether the school representative has authority to ask the armed actors to leave
convergent_norms: Children's safety and psychosocial well-being should be prioritised
Education should continue for the children of the community
divergent_norms: Whether the armed group are protectors of the community or a protection risk for children
The civilian character of schools versus the armed group's claimed role

trainee_brief.situation: In a post-conflict setting many public facilities remain occupied by armed actors. A primary school serving around 1,000 children (host community and IDPs, mainly adolescents, many with conflict-related trauma) is partially occupied by 40 to 50 fighters with a visible, sustained presence. This creates psychosocial distress, restricted use of the facilities, risk of violence or abuse including sexual violence, erosion of the civilian character of the school, and no humanitarian support to regular education programming. Your organisation is risk-averse: it prohibits programming in militarised environments and any direct engagement with parties to the conflict. You therefore facilitate a negotiation led by school authorities, community representatives and local education officials. The school principal and the parents-teachers association favour a confrontational 'they must leave' approach. A local senior education official has an established relationship with the armed group's commander. Phone contact with the commander failed.
trainee_brief.objective: Support the community-led process so that the armed actors peacefully vacate the school and a safe learning environment is restored for the children, within your institutional constraints.
decision_options: Lead the engagement yourself with the armed group
Back a confrontational community demand that the armed actors leave immediately
Facilitate indirectly through the senior education official as lead negotiator

can_decide: Frame the issue around shared protection concerns (children's safety, psychosocial well-being, education)
Identify and coach legitimate intermediaries (education official, school leadership, parent groups)
Prepare local stakeholders: non-confrontational messaging, framing as a request for support
Agree sequencing: informal in-person contact first, gradual structured discussion over time
Support stakeholders in co-developing relocation options, timelines and role-sharing proposals
Keep your own role facilitative and behind the scenes
must_refer: Any deviation from the agreed messaging or role allocation among stakeholders
Any humanitarian programming or presence while armed actors remain in the school compound
Approving or funding an alternative site for the armed group

red_lines.text: No direct engagement with armed actors
No humanitarian programming in militarised environments (no programming in the presence of armed actors)
Children's safety held firm: minimise their interaction with armed actors throughout
Preserve the civilian character of the school and safe education

counterparts.role: Commander of the armed group occupying part of the school compound
counterparts.persona: Commander of 40-50 fighters in post-conflict setting; sees himself and is seen by his men as a protector of the community and its displaced people. Responsive to his own command structure, not to the school principal. Values recognition of his role and sacrifices; flexible on arrangements if treated with respect.
counterparts.cultural_profile: TO BE AUTHORED BY ICRC TRAINER

decides: Whether his fighters leave the school compound
How quickly and where they move
Whether his men reduce contact with children during the transition
must_consult: His own command structure and fighters, on relocation

motive_candidates: Protecting the community and the displaced people sheltering near the school
Securing a workable base for his men
Being recognised as a legitimate protector rather than an occupier

position.stated: His fighters remain in the school compound.

tactical_reasoning.text: His men need a defensible position; a move is only feasible if an acceptable alternative exists and his command accepts it.

values: Role as protector of the community

hidden_interests.text: He wants his role and sacrifices acknowledged before any request is heard.
He would move if a workable temporary site is offered that his men and command accept.

counterparts.role: School principal and parents-teachers association representatives
counterparts.persona: Protective and frustrated; see the armed presence as an occupation to be ended by demand. Push the negotiator towards confrontation and occasionally act on their own.
counterparts.cultural_profile: TO BE AUTHORED BY ICRC TRAINER

decides: Whether the community backs a confrontational or problem-solving approach
Which relocation options the community can offer
must_consult: Parents and community members, on any shared commitment

position.stated: The armed actors must leave the school immediately.
implicit: They want the school and their children back

tactical_reasoning.text: A firm public demand seems the fastest way to reclaim the school and answer to worried parents.

hidden_interests.text: They must be seen by parents as acting decisively, not accepting the occupation.

stakeholders.role: Local senior education official with an established relationship with the commander; lead negotiator and intermediary
School leadership; favoured confrontation and once approached the armed individuals directly off-script
Parent groups; community sensitization and ownership of the solution
State authorities who strongly discourage engagement with armed actors
stakeholders.red_line_on_counterpart: No visible engagement with armed actors

stakeholders.role: The trainee's own risk-averse organisation, behind the scenes

phases.name: Framing the issue as a shared protection concern
phases.instruction: Community and authorities discuss tangible risks; the trainee keeps the framing off legal and political ground.
phases.trainee_must: Frame around children's safety, psychosocial well-being and continued education

phases.name: Preparing local stakeholders
phases.instruction: Prepare school leadership and parents for a respectful, non-accusatory request.
phases.counterpart_says: Use soft and polite words… asking for support rather than telling them what to do.
phases.trainee_must: Agree messaging and roles; assign the education official as lead negotiator

phases.name: Gradual, in-person dialogue
phases.instruction: Informal face-to-face contact first, then structured discussion, with regular follow-ups over about two months.
phases.trainee_must: Keep sensitive discussion in person rather than by phone; allow time and face-saving

phases.name: Co-developing the relocation arrangement
phases.instruction: Discussion shifts from whether the armed actors leave to how relocation can realistically take place.
phases.trainee_must: Explore alternative temporary sites, feasible timelines and shared roles; minimise interactions with children

triggers.say: That was not a good approach and that might create a certain kind of conflict. We shouldn't be considered as a source of this sort of conflict...
It belongs to all of us.
The armed actors considered that the school representative was not considering them as protectors of the community.
triggers.effect: The commander engages and begins to discuss conditions for a move.
The armed actors refuse further contact; the process stalls and risks escalation.

outcomes.label: Armed actors relocate peacefully and the school reopens
Agreement to reduce contact with children and discuss relocation; vacating still pending
Process breaks down and tensions escalate

indicators: Frames the issue around children's safety rather than legal or political disputes
Uses trusted local intermediaries with credibility and access
Supports community ownership of the solution
Frames the issue as a request for support rather than a demand
Acknowledges the armed group's perception of its own role as protectors of the community
Keeps a consistent, agreed message and clear role assignment among stakeholders
Avoids uncoordinated or confrontational approaches that could derail the process
Co-develops practical options such as alternative site, timelines and roles rather than imposing a solution
Preserves relationships and avoids escalation with the armed actors
Keeps the humanitarian actor behind the scenes within institutional constraints
